title: Etiquette around the world
blurb: Tipping, table manners and gift customs, country by country, so you don't put a foot wrong.

items.name: Japan
items.what: Quiet, polite and orderly; small courtesies matter.

facts.v: Not done; it can confuse staff.
Don't stand chopsticks upright in rice or pass food chopstick to chopstick. Slurping noodles is fine. Say 'itadakimasu' before eating.
Bow on greeting. Give and receive gifts and business cards with both hands; avoid sets of four.

items.name: South Korea
items.what: Respect for age shapes everything at the table.

facts.v: Not expected.
Wait for the eldest to start. Pour for others, not yourself, and turn your head away from elders when you drink.
A slight bow, often with a handshake. Use both hands to give and receive; don't write names in red ink.

items.name: Mainland China
items.what: Hospitality is generous, and saving face matters.

facts.v: Not customary, except in top hotels.
The host orders and pays; it's polite to offer to pay. Toast with 'ganbei' and leave a little food to show you're full.
Gifts may be politely refused before being accepted. Avoid clocks (送鐘 sounds like attending a funeral), umbrellas, pears and the number four.

items.name: Hong Kong
items.what: Fast, efficient and very food-focused.

facts.v: Restaurants usually add a 10% service charge; round up taxis.
Tap two fingers on the table to say thanks when someone pours your tea. Dishes are shared.
Lai see red packets at Lunar New Year, given with both hands. Avoid clocks and fours.

items.name: Taiwan
items.what: Warm and courteous, with Chinese customs similar to Hong Kong's.

facts.v: Not expected; hotels and upscale restaurants add 10% service.
Don't stick chopsticks upright in rice. Night-market eating on the go is normal.
Similar gift taboos to China: no clocks, umbrellas or sets of four.

items.wiki: Flag of the Republic of China

items.name: Thailand
items.what: Calm, smiling and respectful, especially of the monarchy and Buddhism.

facts.v: Not required; small tips and rounding up are appreciated.
Eat with a spoon in the right hand, using the fork to push food; chopsticks are for noodles.
Greet with a wai (palms together). Don't touch anyone's head or point your feet at people or Buddha images. Never criticise the royal family; it's illegal.

items.name: Singapore
items.what: Orderly, multicultural and rule-abiding.

facts.v: Not expected; bills include a 10% service charge plus GST.
At hawker centres, a tissue packet on a seat means it's reserved ('chope').
Handshakes are common. Fines are real: no littering, eating on the MRT or selling chewing gum.

items.name: India
items.what: Hospitable, with big regional and religious differences.

facts.v: About 10% in restaurants if no service charge is added.
Eat with your right hand. Many people are vegetarian; Hindus avoid beef and Muslims avoid pork.
Greet with namaste. Give and receive with the right hand; avoid leather gifts for Hindus and alcohol for Muslims.

items.name: Vietnam
items.what: Friendly and family-centred, with Confucian respect for elders.

facts.v: Not expected but appreciated in tourist areas.
Wait for the eldest to start; pick up your bowl to eat rice.
Use both hands to give. Avoid giving handkerchiefs, sharp objects or anything black.

groups.name: Europe
groups.intro: Cheek kisses, bread etiquette and service charges.

items.name: France
items.what: Formal politeness opens every door.

facts.v: Service is included ('service compris'); leave small change for good service.
Say 'bonjour' entering any shop. Bread goes on the table, not the plate; keep your hands on the table.
Friends greet with la bise (cheek kisses). Bring flowers or chocolates, not chrysanthemums (funerals).

items.name: Italy
items.what: Food rules are taken seriously.

facts.v: A 'coperto' cover charge is on the bill; tipping is optional rounding.
Cappuccino is a morning drink; no parmesan on seafood pasta; don't cut spaghetti.
Cheek kisses among friends; dress smartly.

items.name: United Kingdom
items.what: Polite, understated and keen on queues.

facts.v: 10–12.5% in restaurants, often added as a service charge; none at the pub bar.
At the pub, groups buy drinks in 'rounds'. Never jump a queue.
A handshake; small talk about the weather is a genuine national pastime.

items.name: Germany
items.what: Punctual, direct and orderly.

facts.v: Round up 5–10%, telling the server the total as you pay rather than leaving it on the table.
Say 'Prost' and look people in the eye when clinking glasses.
A firm handshake; be on time. Shops close on Sundays.

items.name: Spain
items.what: Relaxed and social, and it runs late.

facts.v: Small change or rounding up.
Lunch is around 2–4 pm and dinner from 9 pm or later. Tapas are for sharing.
Two cheek kisses among friends.

items.name: United States
items.what: Friendly and informal, with tipping built into wages.

facts.v: 18–22% at restaurants is expected; about US$1–2 a drink at bars.
Portions are big and taking leftovers home is normal.
A firm handshake and first names quickly.

items.name: Mexico
items.what: Warm, family-oriented and festive.

facts.v: 10–15% in restaurants.
Lunch is the main meal, often late afternoon.
A handshake, or a cheek kiss among friends.

items.name: Brazil
items.what: Warm, physical and relaxed about time.

facts.v: A 10% service charge is usually on the bill.
Use a knife and fork even for pizza.
Hugs and cheek kisses; the 'OK' hand sign is rude there.

items.name: United Arab Emirates
items.what: Very hospitable, modern and respectful of Islamic customs.

facts.v: 10–15% is appreciated if not included.
Eat and pass with your right hand. During Ramadan, be discreet about eating and drinking in public in daylight.
Wait for a woman to offer her hand. Don't give alcohol or pork products.

items.wiki: Flag of the United Arab Emirates

items.name: Morocco
items.what: Hospitable, with mint tea offered as welcome.

facts.v: About 10% in restaurants; small tips for services are expected.
Eat from the shared dish with your right hand, using bread to scoop.
Accept the mint tea. During Ramadan, avoid eating in public in daylight.

items.name: Türkiye
items.what: Generous hosts; tea is offered everywhere.

facts.v: 5–10% in restaurants.
Accept the tea (çay). Take your shoes off when entering a home.
Bring sweets like baklava or Turkish delight when visiting.
